newsitem.title: RWANDA: Commander says multinational Zaire force no threat.
newsitem.headline: Commander says multinational Zaire force no threat.

text.p: The Canadian commander of a proposed multinational relief force for eastern Zaire said on Wednesday the force was no threat to anyone despite Rwandan objections.

Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril told reporters on arrival in Kigali from Entebbe airport, Uganda -- expected to be the force's main base -- that he was trying to sort out priorities in the wake of the return of up to 600,000 refugees to Rwanda.
"We're trying to make up our minds what the real situation is," said Baril. "It's very urgent we make a real picture of where we are going."

Asked what was the point of meeting Rwandan military strongman Paul Kagame when Kigali had said it was opposed to the force operating from its territory, the general said: "That's what I'm coming to discuss...It's very, very clear we are coming for a humanitarian mission -- no threat to anyone, no political taking sides."

Baril first met the 19 members of a Canadian military liasion team in Kigali and officers from Britain and the United States which have both been trying by aerial photographs to locate large masses of refugees in Zaire scattered by fighting.
A Canadian military spokesman and Rwandan officials said Baril would hold his key talks with Kagame, who is vice president and defence minister, later on Wednesday evening.
The Rwandan government says any multinational force for Zaire is irrelevant because most of the refugees have returned and Kigali is concerned about the force's mandate and composition.
Rwandan officials have said the force cannot use Rwandan territory for its operations since the return of a flood of refugees in five days starting on November 15.

"The problem with the multinational force is it was approved before the half a million refugees returned," said a diplomat in Kigali. "Now we have to find out where exactly the rest are, how many of them are there and what they need."
Uganda's foreign ministry said on Wednesday the government had agreed to the use of Entebbe airport as a base for international relief operations in the eastern Zaire crisis.

Canada, impatient with the indecision on the eastern Zaire refugee crisis, on Tuesday proposed a military headquarters for relief operations in Uganda. U.S. and British teams also operate from Entebbe.
The Rwandan government says any aid would best be used within Rwandan territory, providing for the new returnees.
But aid agencies say a multinational force is still needed to help reach hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees and Zaireans displaced by the fighting outside rebel-held areas of eastern Zaire.
Talks in Stuttgart at the weekend between potential Western contributors to the force agreed on various options for the force and passed them back to the governments concerned for a decision.
Baril stays in Kigali overnight and was hoping to travel on Thursday to the eastern Zairean city of Goma, held by Rwanda-backed rebels who reject any multinational force for Zaire.
Baril, 52, the commander of Canada's ground forces who was appointed to head the multinational humanitarian relief force on November 14, last visited Rwanda's capital last Thursday.

On Wednesday morning, he met Major-General Edwin Smith, the commander of a U.S. assessment team based in Rwanda, and Sergio Viera de Mello, the U.N. humanitarian coordinator for the Great Lakes region, at Entebbe airport before flying on to Kigali.
A U.N. official, who declined to be identified, said he expected even if a multinational force was formed it would not be charged with protecting aid workers deep inside Zaire.

"In Zaire, foreign troops could help with logistics, ground support and I suppose a modicum of other services like engineering -- the sort of things that soldiers can do quite successfully -- with a degree of self-protection," he added.

"We are not talking about a multinational force deploying in an operational sense with combat toops but we might be talking about something different with a lower profile and more logistics-oriented with an airlift," the U.N. official said.

The U.S. assessment team, using photographs of eastern Zaire taken from a surveillance aircraft, said last Saturday there were only 202,000 refugees left in eastern Zaire and an estimated 600,000 Rwandan refugees had flooded back to Rwanda.
